## Per-chapter highlights

### Chapter 1 — The Burnt Offering (Olah)

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, messianic-prophecy, restoration

Leviticus opens with the LORD calling Moses from the Tabernacle just completed at the close of Exodus, and gives the first of five offering- types: the burnt offering (olah, "ascending"). A male without blemish from the herd, flock, or fowl, voluntarily offered, with the offerer's hand laid on its head; the whole animal consumed on the altar as "a sweet savour unto the LORD." The chapter establishes the foundational pattern — substitutionary atonement and total devotion to God — that the rest of the sacrificial system builds on.

### Chapter 2 — The Meal Offering (Minchah)

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

The meal offering (minchah) — the chapter's bloodless grain offering of fine flour, oil, and frankincense, brought raw or baked in oven, pan, or fryingpan, always with salt, never with leaven or honey. A "memorial portion" is burned on the altar as a sweet savour; the remainder belongs to Aaron and his sons as "a thing most holy." The chapter's salt-of-the-covenant provision and the bloodless-offering category fill in what the burnt offering of Lev 1 left unspecified.

### Chapter 3 — The Peace Offering (Zevach Shelamim)

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

The peace offering (zevach shelamim) — male or female of herd, flock, or goats, without blemish; hand laid on its head, blood sprinkled, the fat and kidneys and the caul above the liver burned on the altar as "the food of the offering made by fire... a sweet savour." The chapter's signature provision: all the fat belongs to the LORD; the fat and the blood may never be eaten. The peace offering is the shared-meal sacrifice — portions for God, the priest, and the offerer's family eat together before the LORD.

### Chapter 4 — The Sin Offering (Chattat), Graduated by Office

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, messianic-prophecy, restoration

The sin offering (chattat) — graduated by office and responsibility: the anointed priest brings a bullock (his sin defiles the sanctuary); the whole congregation a bullock (corporate sin); a ruler a male goat; a common person a female goat or lamb. For sins of ignorance ("through ignorance against any of the commandments"). The priest's and congregation's offerings have their bodies burned outside the camp — the pattern Hebrews 13:11-13 reads as fulfilled in Christ "suffered without the gate."

### Chapter 5 — The Trespass Offering (Asham), Restitution Plus One-Fifth

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, restoration

Specific instances triggering the trespass offering (failure to testify when called as witness, contact with uncleanness, rash oaths); the offering's three-tier accessibility (lamb, two birds, fine flour) accommodating the poor. The asham (trespass offering) proper: a ram with restitution-plus-one-fifth for inadvertent sin against "the holy things of the LORD" — the OT's first explicit combination of sacrifice with monetary reparation, anticipating the broader restitution principle of Lev 6.

### Chapter 6 — Priest's Manual: Trespass Concluded; Perpetual Fire; Offerings' Procedure

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

The trespass-offering legislation concludes (now covering deception of neighbor: restitution-plus-one-fifth, then offering). The chapter then turns to the priests with a manual of procedure for the offerings — the burnt offering's perpetual altar fire that "shall ever be burning... it shall never go out"; the meal offering eaten by the priests as their portion; the daily perpetual meal-offering of the anointed priest; the sin offering's most-holy character.

### Chapter 7 — Priest's Manual Concluded; Peace Offering Sub-Types; Priestly Portions

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

The priest's manual concludes. The trespass offering's priestly procedure; the burnt-offering skin and meal-offering remainder as priestly portions; the peace offering's three sub-types (thanksgiving, vow, freewill) with their timing requirements; the fat-and-blood prohibition restated; the wave-breast and heave- shoulder priestly portions; and the chapter's closing summary that closes the entire offerer-and-priest manual block (Lev 1-7).

### Chapter 8 — Consecration of Aaron and His Sons (Seven Days)

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration, prophetic-call

Moses carries out the consecration of Aaron and his sons that Exodus 29 had prescribed. The whole congregation gathers; Aaron is washed, robed (with breastplate and Urim and Thummim), and anointed; his sons clothed and anointed; the bullock sin offering, the burnt-offering ram, and the consecration ram each killed with the prescribed blood-applications including the right ear, right thumb, and right great toe. The seven-day stay at the tent door begins. The chapter executes what Exodus 29 commanded; obedience is total.

### Chapter 9 — The Eighth Day: Fire from the LORD Consumes the Offerings

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration, prophetic-call

The eighth day after the seven-day consecration: Aaron offers his first sacrifices as installed high priest — sin offering and burnt offering for himself, then the same with peace offerings for the people. He lifts up his hand and blesses the people; Moses and Aaron enter the tent, return, and bless again — and the glory of the LORD appears. Fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes the burnt offering on the altar; the people shout and fall on their faces. The sacrificial system is divinely accepted.

### Chapter 10 — Nadab and Abihu: Strange Fire

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, prophetic-call

Aaron's two eldest sons offer "strange fire" before the LORD — fire He did not command — and are consumed by fire from the LORD on the spot. Moses' explanation: "I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me, and before all the people I will be glorified." Aaron holds his peace. The chapter closes with the wine-prohibition for priests on duty and the priestly responsibility to teach the difference between holy and unholy, clean and unclean — the catastrophe re-orienting the priesthood to its discernment-vocation.

### Chapter 11 — Clean and Unclean Animals

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

Israel's dietary purity laws. Land animals must part the hoof and chew the cud (so the camel, hare, coney, and swine are excluded); water creatures must have fins and scales; an extensive list of unclean birds; the creeping things prohibited. The chapter's theological grounding (11:44-45): "ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy." The food-rules embody at the table the holiness-distinction the priesthood is to teach.

### Chapter 12 — Purification After Childbirth

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

The mother's purification ritual after childbirth — seven days of uncleanness plus thirty-three of purifying for a son (with eighth- day circumcision), fourteen plus sixty-six for a daughter, then a burnt offering (lamb) and sin offering (pigeon); the pigeon-pair for the poor. Mary and Joseph's offering of "two turtledoves, or two young pigeons" at Jesus' presentation (Luke 2:24) signals the holy family's economic class as the chapter's poor-provision recipients.

### Chapter 13 — Diagnosis of Tzaraat (Leprosy)

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, restoration

The diagnostic procedures for tzaraat — the broad OT category KJV translates "leprosy" but which covers skin diseases, garment-mildew, and (in the next chapter) house-mildew. The priest examines, quarantines for seven days, re-examines, and pronounces clean or unclean. The chapter's distinctive paradox: a body completely white with the affliction is pronounced clean (13:12-13). The diagnosed leper lives outside the camp, with rent clothes and bare head, crying "Unclean, unclean" — the social isolation that the NT healings of lepers reverse.

### Chapter 14 — Cleansing of Tzaraat

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration, atonement

The cleansing ritual once tzaraat is healed: the two-bird rite outside the camp (one killed over running water, one released alive), washing-and-shaving, a seven-day liminal period, the eighth-day trespass / sin / burnt offerings with blood and oil on the right ear, thumb, and toe — and the poor person's reduced-cost version. The chapter then extends the same logic to house-tzaraat. NT echo: Christ's leper-healings (Matt 8:1-4, Luke 17:11-19) presuppose this chapter's procedure.

### Chapter 15 — Bodily Discharges

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

The chapter's chiastic treatment of bodily-fluid discharges: abnormal male discharge (15:2-15), normal male emission and marital relations (15:16-18), normal menstruation (15:19-24), abnormal female discharge (15:25-30). The chapter closes with its theological rationale (15:31): separating Israel from uncleanness so the sanctuary is not defiled. NT echo: the woman with the twelve-year issue touching Jesus' garment (Mark 5:25-34) — the chapter's framework reversed in the same touch-direction inversion as the leper-healings.

### Chapter 16 — The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur)

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, atonement, restoration, prophetic-call

The structural and theological centerpiece of Leviticus. Once a year on the tenth of the seventh month, the high priest enters beyond the veil with bullock-blood for himself and goat-blood for the people, sprinkling on the kapporet (mercy seat); a second goat — for Azazel — bears the people's confessed sins into the wilderness. The chapter's NT trajectory: Christ as the once-for-all high priest and offering (Heb 9-10); the temple veil torn at His death (Matt 27:50-51); 3 Ne 9:19-20's Lehite-Bountiful announcement that sacrifices are done away.

### Chapter 17 — Blood and Atonement; Holiness Code Begins

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, atonement

The chapter that opens the Holiness Code (Lev 17-26). All domestic-animal slaughter must be at the door of the tabernacle; no more sacrifices to seirim (goat-demons of the wilderness). The chapter's theological center is 17:11 — "the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls" — the OT's clearest single statement of the blood-atonement principle that underlies all the sacrificial chapters. NT echo at Acts 15:20-29 (the Jerusalem Council's blood-prohibition for Gentile converts).

### Chapter 18 — Sexual Ethics; The Land That Vomits

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, holiness

Israel must not walk after the practices of Egypt or Canaan. An extended incest catalogue (18:6-18), followed by prohibitions on adultery, child-sacrifice to Molech, male homosexual intercourse, and bestiality (18:19-23). The chapter's framing warning: the previous inhabitants of the land were vomited out for these practices, and Israel will be too if it does them (18:24-30). The chapter installs the OT's foundational sexual-ethics catalogue.

### Chapter 19 — Love Thy Neighbour; The Holiness Code's Heart

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, holiness, restoration

The Holiness Code's chiastic and theological center. Opening with "Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy" (19:2), the chapter weaves together cult, family, agrarian provision for the poor, weights and measures, judicial fairness, care for the deaf and blind and aged and sojourner, and — at 19:18 — "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," picked up by Christ as the second great commandment (Matt 22:39) and called the royal law (Jas 2:8). Sixteen times the chapter closes prohibitions with "I am the LORD."

### Chapter 20 — Penalties for Sexual Sin and Idolatry

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, holiness

The penalty-list paired with Lev 18's prohibitions: capital punishment for child-sacrifice to Molech, cursing father or mother, adultery, incest, male homosexual intercourse, bestiality, and traffic with familiar spirits. The chapter closes with the land-vomits warning (now in second person — "the land vomit you not out also") and the separation-rationale: Israel has been "severed from other people" to be the LORD's own. The chapter completes the Lev 18-19-20 triptych at the Holiness Code's center.

### Chapter 21 — Priestly Holiness

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, holiness

Restrictions on the priests beyond those of the people: limits on mourning-defilement for the dead, prohibition on pagan mutilation practices, marriage restrictions, and (for the high priest) the most stringent rules. A separate cluster (21:16-23) excludes physically blemished priests from altar-service while preserving their right to eat the holy food. The chapter installs the OT's holiness-graduations within the priesthood.

### Chapter 22 — Holy Things and Acceptable Offerings

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, holiness

Three clusters of holy-thing rules: priests in uncleanness must abstain from holy food until cleansed (22:1-9); the priestly food may be eaten only by the priest's household proper (22:10-16); sacrificial animals offered to the LORD must be without physical blemish (22:17-25), with the chapter closing on age-rules, mother-and-young provision, and thanksgiving-eaten-same-day. The chapter's blemish-exclusion parallels Lev 21's priestly-blemish exclusion: offerer and offering alike must reflect the LORD's wholeness.

### Chapter 23 — The Festal Calendar

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration, prophetic-call

The OT's most comprehensive single festal calendar: weekly sabbath; the spring cluster (Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Pentecost / Weeks); the fall cluster (Trumpets, Day of Atonement, Tabernacles). The chapter's typological NT trajectory: Passover and Firstfruits fulfilled in Christ's death and resurrection (1 Cor 15:20-23); Pentecost in the Acts 2 outpouring; Tabernacles invoked at John 7:37-39's "If any man thirst." The seven feasts together compose Israel's liturgical year.

### Chapter 24 — Lamps, Showbread, Blasphemy, Lex Talionis

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment

Three brief sanctuary-maintenance rules (the perpetual oil for the lamps, the twelve loaves of weekly showbread, the rules for blasphemy) frame a narrative interlude — the only narrative passage in Leviticus 17-26 — in which a half- Israelite son who blasphemed the Name is stoned outside the camp. The chapter's lex talionis passage (24:17-22, eye for eye, tooth for tooth) installs the OT's principle of proportional retribution applied equally to stranger and homeborn.
